## Knowledge base excerpts
[1] Responding to repeated questions
It's very common for a person with dementia to ask the same question many times in a short period, because they genuinely don't remember having asked or been answered before. Getting frustrated or pointing out that they already asked usually causes distress without helping. Instead, answer calmly and briefly each time, as if it were the first time. If a question reflects anxiety (like repeatedly asking when a family member is arriving), try addressing the underlying feeling — reassurance, a clock or written note they can refer to, or a distracting activity can help more than a factual answer alone. Writing key information on a whiteboard in a shared space can also reduce how often the same question needs to be asked.

## Knowledge base excerpts
[1] When to see a doctor: warning signs
While dementia symptoms generally progress gradually, some changes warrant a prompt call to the doctor rather than waiting for the next scheduled visit. These include a sudden, sharp increase in confusion (which can indicate a urinary tract infection or other acute illness, not just disease progression), new or worsening hallucinations, a fall or head injury, signs of pain that can't be verbally described, sudden changes in mobility or swallowing, or a significant, unexplained mood or behavior shift. Sudden changes are especially important to flag quickly, since they're more often caused by a treatable medical issue than by the dementia itself.

[2] Medication management tips for caregivers
As dementia progresses, most people can no longer manage their own medications safely and need a caregiver to take over. Use a pill organizer sorted by day and time, keep an up-to-date written list of all medications and dosages for appointments and emergencies, and store medication securely out of reach if the patient might take extra doses by mistake. Track doses taken versus missed so patterns are easy to spot. Never adjust a dosage or stop a medication without consulting the prescribing doctor, even if a dose seems to be causing side effects — call the doctor's office instead. Bring the full medication list to every medical appointment.

[3] Preparing for a doctor's appointment
Getting the most out of a medical appointment takes some preparation. Bring an updated medication list, a short written summary of any new symptoms, behavior changes, falls, or concerns since the last visit, and specific questions you want answered, since it's easy to forget them in the moment. If possible, request extra time or a caregiver-focused portion of the visit, since some things are easier to discuss without the patient present, and some may be worth discussing with the patient in the room to keep them included. Bring someone else along if you can, both for support and as a second set of ears.
